newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenyan air controllers strike goes on.
newsitem.headline: Kenyan air controllers strike goes on.

text.p: Kenyan air traffic controllers on Wednesday defied a government order to return to work and industry officials said flights in and out of the country were running up to two hours late.
The controllers went on strike on Saturday to press for a 50-fold pay rise the government says it cannot afford.
On Tuesday the government of President Daniel arap Moi gave them an ultimatum to return to work by 4 p.m. (1300 GMT) or be sacked. The strikers ignored the threat.
"There will be no negotiations with the strikers," a ministry of transport and communications spokeswoman said.
"We (the government) stand by our earlier order, that those who would not have returned to work would be considered deserters. We are hoping the strike will fizzle out."
She did not say whether the strikers had been sacked. Aviation industry sources said there were very few air traffic controllers in Kenya and the government would be forced to negotiate.

Industry sources also said the continued strike posed a security threat in Kenya's skies. They said that it was dangerous for planes to continue circling around Nairobi or the port of Mombasa while awaiting clearance to land.
A spokesman at national carrier Kenya Airways estimated delays of 30 minutes to an hour but other airlines said international flights were delayed two hours on average.
Industry officials said meteorological workers planned to join the strike.
"A meteorological department strike would complicate it. The weather is important for take-off," one airline official said.
But the official said the meteorological department had not formally declared its role in the strike.
Civil aviation authorities have replaced the strikers with instructors and administrators who are short of practical experience.
A ministry spokesman said the controllers wanted basic salaries increased to 261,510 shillings ($4,670) from 5,000 shillings ($90) a month.
